title: How Crime-Scene Clean-up Works
summary: Josh and Chuck discuss crime scene cleanup (CTSDecon, crime and trauma scene decontamination), based on a HowStuffWorks article by Julia Layton. They cover how the work differs from movies like Curdled and Sunshine Cleaning, the emotional demands and burnout, typical scenes (violent death, decomposition, meth lab cleanup), the equipment used, decomposition and maggot removal, disposal rules and incineration, training and gross-out testing, pricing and insurance or victim-reparation funding, marketing, and the ethics of profiting from tragedy. The episode ends with listener mail, the second part of a prison email from a former inmate describing commissary economics, escapes, and prison slang.

Stuff You Should Know listener mail

segments.title: Opening banter and movie comparisons
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck joke about their appearance and discuss the movies Curdled and Sunshine Cleaning, agreeing both are inaccurate about crime scene cleanup.

segments.title: What CTSDecon is and the emotional demands
segments.summary: CTSDecon (crime and trauma scene decontamination) is described as industrial-level cleaning with biohazard gear, aiming to return a scene to its original condition. Workers often come from EMT, nursing, fire, or military backgrounds, and need sympathy without empathy; average tenure is about eight months.
topics: sympathy versus empathy in cleanup work

segments.title: Three main scenes: violent death, decomposition, meth labs
segments.summary: The hosts outline the three main scene types. Meth labs are toxic and require removing drywall, flooring and carpet; construction background helps.

segments.title: Tools of the trade
segments.summary: Equipment includes biohazard suits, biowaste drums, disinfectants, ozone machines, foggers, enzyme solvents, shovels and putty knives for clotted blood and dried brain matter, steamers, no-touch cleaning systems, ladders, and cameras for insurance photos.

segments.title: Decomposing bodies and maggot removal
segments.summary: Decomposition brings bloating, insects, liquefied skin and organs, and a strong ammonia smell. Cleaners must find and remove liquefied remains and maggots, which are burned.

segments.title: Violent death scenes, costs, and disposal rules
segments.summary: Suicide and shooting scenes, especially head shots, produce the most blood. Cleanups can take up to 48 hours and cost roughly one to three thousand dollars per room, with rates around six hundred dollars an hour. Waste must be incinerated under strict permits, with special transport and disposal, and the industry is not nationally regulated.

segments.title: Training, gross-out testing, health risks, and Oklahoma anecdote
segments.summary: Workers are tested for their reaction to gore, including dead animals, and need hepatitis B vaccines. Stress disorders and unsuitable personalities are screened for. Chuck and Josh discuss a friend in Oklahoma who saw meth victims who had eaten dirt.

segments.title: Business, insurance funding, marketing, and ethics of profiting from tragedy
segments.summary: Insurance or crime victim reparations often pay for cleanup. Companies market to hotels, motels, detectives and ambulance drivers. The hosts debate whether profiting from tragedy is acceptable, citing Neil Smithers Crime Scene Cleaners in San Francisco.

segments.title: Listener mail: prison email part two and sign-off
segments.summary: Hosts read part two of a listener's prison email covering commissary goods as currency, handball tournaments, two escapes, and prison slang such as shank, the shoe, keying stuff, and man walking. The episode closes with the email address and website pointers.
